chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Ja'far, from Al-Husayn ibn Malik, who said:

I wrote to Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him), 'Know, my Master, that the son of a brother of mine died, so he bequeathed to my Master a place, and he bequeathed that everything in his house should be handed over, even the pegs, to be sold, and the price be given to my Master, and he bequeathed for Hajj, and he bequeathed for the poor from his family, and he bequeathed to his aunt and his sister with wealth. So I looked, and found that what he bequeathed was more than one-third, and perhaps it was close to half of what he left, and he left behind a son of his who was three years old, and left debts. So what is your view, my Master?'
So he (peace be upon him) signed: 'Limit his bequest to one-third of his wealth, and distribute that among those he bequeathed to according to the measure of their shares, if Allah wills.'

key_terms.أَوْتَاد: Pegs (used for securing tents, indicating even small household items were included)
key_terms.الثُّلُث: One-third (the maximum portion of an estate that can be bequeathed to non-heirs)

ai.seo_question: How are bequests distributed when they exceed one-third of the estate in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the mechanism of proportional reduction (tanqis) when bequests exceed the permissible one-third limit, ensuring fairness among multiple legatees. It highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that debts and heirs take precedence, and the remaining one-third is distributed to beneficiaries according to their allocated shares, reflecting the practical application of estate law in early Islamic society.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, fromo Abdullah Bin Ja’far, from Al Husayn Bin Maalik who said,

‘I wrote to Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup>, ‘Know, my Master<sup>asws</sup>, that the son of a brother of mine dies, so he bequeathed to my Master with a place, and bequeathed that everything in his house should be handed over, even the pegs to be sold, and the price be made to my Master<sup>asws</sup>, and bequeathed with a Hajj, and bequeathed for the poor from his family, and bequeathed for his mother and his sister with wealth. So I looked, so that which he had bequeathed with was more than the third, and perhaps it was near to the half from what he had left (legacy), and he left behind a son of his of three years old, and left debts. So give me your<sup>asws</sup> view, of my Master<sup>asws</sup>’.

So he<sup>asws</sup> signed: ‘Reduce his bequest to be upon the third from his wealth, and distribute that between the ones he bequeathed for upon the measurement of their share, Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Willing’.
en.sarwar: 13. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from ‘Abd Allah ibn Ja‘far from al-Husayn ibn Malik who has narrated the following: “I once wrote to abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, saying, ’My master, I inform you that the son of my brother has died and has made a will about a certain piece of property for you.

He in his will has said that everything in his house must be given, even the pegs must be sold and the price sent to my master. He has made a will for al-Hajj. He has made a will for the poor of his family, for his aunt, for his sister to receive a certain amount of property and I have considered it to be more than one-third, perhaps about one-half of his legacy, and he has left behind a son who is three years old. He has left debts to pay. I want to know your opinion, my master, in the matter.’
He (the Imam) signed the answer that said, ‘His will must be limited within one-third of his legacy and it will be divided among the beneficiaries proportionate to each one’s share.’”
